The Work, Torah Thought and Legacy of Rabbi Avraham de Boton (Author of the "Lechem Mishneh")
His Life and Era: The Golden Age in Ottoman Salonika
During the 16th century the city of Salonika, under Ottoman rule, served as the most prominent spiritual, economic and halakhic center of the diaspora of those expelled from Spain [cite: 1]. The arrival of thousands of scholars and families from Spanish and Portuguese Jewry breathed new life into the local community and turned Salonika into a city of yeshivot, Hebrew printing houses and rabbinic courts whose rulings spread across the entire Jewish world [cite: 1]. In an environment rich in Torah scholars and stormy halakhic discussions grew Rabbi Chiya Avraham son of Rabbi Moshe de Boton [cite: 1]. The period was marked by tremendous efforts to organize, codify and interpret Jewish law, owing to the communities' severance from their historical centers on the Iberian Peninsula and the need to provide a legal and administrative response to the new challenges of life in the Ottoman exile [cite: 1]. The Torah work of Rabbi Avraham de Boton grew precisely in this dynamic space, in which the sages were required to create a synthesis between the depth of Sephardic theoretical study and the ability to carry out practical halakhic ruling in communities teeming with commerce and learning [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Rabbi Chiya Avraham de Boton was born in Salonika in the 40s of the 16th century (around 5305 / 1545) to a distinguished family descended from those expelled from Spain [cite: 1, 4]. The name "Chiya" was added to his original name "Avraham" during a severe illness that struck him in the days of his life, as a remedy for healing and long life, and so he would at times sign his name in his works and rulings [cite: 1]. Despite his lofty standing and his recognition as one of the sages of Salonika, a head of a yeshiva and a central halakhic authority, his life was relatively short [cite: 1, 2]. He died young, apparently at the age of only 43, while a severe epidemic raged in his city [cite: 1, 2]. The year of his death accepted in scholarship and tradition is 5348 (1588), although in certain sources there are later proposals for the 90s of the 16th century [cite: 1, 5]. He was buried in the ancient Jewish cemetery of Salonika [cite: 1].
A popular historical legend became attached to his death and burial, attesting to the reverence and admiration that the members of his community felt for him. According to the tradition, Rabbi Avraham died on a Friday, and his burial ended very close to sunset, so that the mourners feared they had entered a doubt of Shabbat desecration [cite: 1]. The deep grief of the community members subsided when, immediately after the burial, the sun emerged from behind the clouds and it became clear that Shabbat had not yet begun [cite: 1]. Rabbi Avraham de Boton left behind a glorious Torah dynasty [cite: 1]. His sons – Rabbi Meir de Boton (author of "Responsa Maharam de Boton"), Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Aharon – also served in rabbinic and halakhic roles in the Ottoman Empire [cite: 1, 3, 6]. His descendants and sons-in-law, among them the wealthy Yitzchak Algranti, were later involved in the publication and preservation of his Torah legacy at the printing house in Izmir and in other communities [cite: 3].
The Salonikan Study Hall: His Teachers and Students
The Torah development of Rabbi Avraham de Boton rests on the foundations of the glorious study hall of Salonika in the 16th century [cite: 1, 2]. His foremost and principal teacher was Rabbi Shmuel de Medina, known by the acronym the Maharashdam – one of the greatest sages of Salonika, the halakhic authority of the generation and the spiritual leader of the community [cite: 1, 2, 5]. The Maharashdam bequeathed to his student the analytical approach to study, characterized by strict textual precision, by examining the sources of the Talmud and the Rishonim with critical eyes, and by a constant striving for a halakhic decision anchored in economic and social reality [cite: 1, 2, 7]. Rabbi Avraham's attachment to his teacher was extremely deep, and the teaching of the Maharashdam forms a central foundation in the responsa and commentaries of the author of the "Lechem Mishneh" [cite: 1, 2, 7].
As a rabbi and head of a yeshiva in Salonika, Rabbi Avraham de Boton raised many students who continued his path of study and held rabbinic positions throughout the Ottoman Empire [cite: 1]. Among his prominent students mentioned in the literature of the generation are Rabbi Shmuel Chayon, one of the sages of Salonika who continued his teacher's tradition of study in teaching and ruling, and Rabbi Shabtai Yona, a respected author and halakhic authority who spread his teacher's teaching throughout the communities [cite: 1]. In historical literature, such as the book "Koreh HaDorot" by Rabbi David Conforte, a claim is cited in the name of Rabbi Mordechai Kalai that he wrote parts of the "Lechem Mishneh" commentary in partnership with him [cite: 1]. However, scholars and commentators note that this claim is not supported by additional sources and does not reflect the unique creation of the author of the work [cite: 1].
His Central Work: "Lechem Mishneh" on the Mishneh Torah of the Rambam
The work that secured Rabbi Avraham de Boton his immortal place in the Torah canon is his book "Lechem Mishneh," a comprehensive and deep commentary on the Rambam's great work, the "Mishneh Torah" [cite: 1, 2, 8]. The process of composing the "Lechem Mishneh" includes a bibliographic and dramatic chapter in the history of the literature of the commentators on the Rambam [cite: 1, 9, 10]. Rabbi Avraham began to compose his work as an independent commentary whose aim was to locate the talmudic sources of the Rambam's rulings, to resolve the objections of the Raavad (Rabbi Avraham ben David of Posquières), and to explain difficult perplexities in the Rambam's language [cite: 1, 8, 11].
While immersed in writing the work, the commentary of our master Rabbi Yosef Karo, the "Kesef Mishneh," which was printed at that time, came into his hands [cite: 1, 9, 10]. Once he became aware that Rabbi Yosef Karo had already dealt extensively with locating the sources and answering the Raavad's objections, Rabbi Avraham de Boton made a far-reaching editorial decision. He omitted from his manuscript all the explanations and sources already cited in the "Kesef Mishneh," and focused solely on topics, contradictions and difficulties that Rabbi Yosef Karo had not dealt with or had left with "requires further study" (tzarikh iyun) [cite: 9, 10, 12]. As a result, his book turned from a merely foundational explanation into a concentrated, deep and dialectical work, which complements the "Kesef Mishneh" – and hence also derives its name: "Lechem Mishneh," as an expression of a double portion and an addition to the commentary of Maran [cite: 9, 10, 12].
The interpretive method of the "Lechem Mishneh" rests on several central theoretical principles. First, it focuses on harmonization and the resolution of internal contradictions in the Rambam. Whereas earlier commentators sometimes tended to attribute changes of wording in the Rambam to repetitions or copying errors, Rabbi Avraham de Boton took as a basic premise that the Rambam was precise in every word [cite: 8, 13]. He developed brilliant distinguishing mechanisms to resolve contradictions between different laws in the book "Mishneh Torah," such as resolving the contradiction between the Rambam's attitude to the Greek language in the Laws of Tefillin and the law he cites in the Laws of Megillah [cite: 8, 13].
Second, in places where the "Kesef Mishneh" did not find an explicit source in the Babylonian Talmud, the "Lechem Mishneh" displays extensive mastery of the Jerusalem Talmud, the Tosefta, the halakhic Midrashim and the structure of talmudic topics, and extracts by the power of the depth of dialectic the exact source [cite: 8]. Third, regarding the Raavad's objections, Rabbi Avraham is not content with rejecting the objection, but penetrates deeply into the Raavad's reasoning and formulates the dispute between him and the Rambam as a whole conceptual-halakhic unit [cite: 11, 14].
Comparison Criterion | Maggid Mishneh (Rabbi Vidal of Tolosa) [cite: 1] | Kesef Mishneh (Rabbi Yosef Karo) [cite: 1, 8, 9] | Lechem Mishneh (Rabbi Avraham de Boton) [cite: 1, 8, 9]
Time and Place | 14th century, Spain [cite: 1] | 16th century, Land of Israel / Turkey [cite: 1, 8] | 16th century, Salonika [cite: 1, 8]
Main Goal | Revealing the talmudic source and explaining the plain meaning of the Rambam [cite: 8] | Encyclopedia of sources and resolution of the Raavad's objections [cite: 1, 8] | Completing the "Kesef Mishneh," resolving contradictions and depth of dialectic [cite: 8, 9, 13]
Study Style | Concise, precise and based on plain meaning | Comprehensive, including comparisons to the Beit Yosef and the Tur | Theoretical-distinguishing, focused on textual and conceptual difficulties [cite: 1, 8]
Methodological Uniqueness | The first classic work written on the Rambam | Almost complete coverage of all parts of the Yad HaChazakah | Focus on subtleties, avoidance of conscious duplication, and care for linguistic precision [cite: 1, 9]
His Halakhic Work: The Responsa "Lechem Rav" and His Method of Ruling
Alongside his interpretive work on the Rambam, Rabbi Avraham de Boton acted as a central halakhic authority and answered hundreds of halakhic questions sent to him from all over the Ottoman Empire [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His responses were gathered in his book "Responsa Lechem Rav" [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The book of questions and answers was not printed in the author's lifetime because of his early death [cite: 2, 3]. The work was brought to the printing house in Izmir in 5420 (1660) by his grandson, the scholar Rabbi Avraham son of Rabbi Aharon de Boton, in partnership with the wealthy Yitzchak Algranti, who was married to the daughter of the author's son [cite: 3]. The printers and descendants dedicated five hundred books from the edition as a binding endowment whose proceeds would be devoted to supporting Torah scholars studying in the yeshivot, a fact that teaches of the communal and scholarly outlook of the family [cite: 3].
The responses of the author of the "Lechem Mishneh" in "Responsa Lechem Rav" reveal a halakhic authority of broad horizons, who combines theoretical depth with attention to the finest details of law and justice [cite: 3, 15, 16]. In his method of ruling, his reliance on the principle of "umdena demuchach" (the evident assessment, an assessment of the intent of the heart) in interpreting documents and conditions stands out. Rabbi Avraham gave great weight to the presumed intention of the parties in transactions and contracts, beyond the strict wording of the words [cite: 15]. In a famous ruling he emphasized that when a person deposits or transfers assets to his fellow in order to cover debts, it is not to be assumed that he intended that fellow to pocket personal profits from the assets, unless this was explicitly stated [cite: 15].
Likewise, in the areas of Choshen Mishpat he gave decisive halakhic validity to merchants' custom (the custom of sitomta), even in situations in which the original talmudic law raises difficulties, such as an obligation concerning something that has not yet come into the world, or asmachta [cite: 16]. His rulings also established the absolute legal power of the public and the communal leaders to obligate themselves and to enter into contracts without a predetermined limit, relying on the special status of public matters in Jewish law [cite: 16]. In addition, his discussions on the topics of "beri veshema" (certainty versus doubt) and the laws of claims and counterclaims show a systematic analysis of the laws of presumptions, with a consistent preference for the presumption in favor of the holder of the money where there is no admissible evidence to contradict it [cite: 17].
Scholars of responsa literature and of the Hebrew language, among them Nachum Sokolow, noted the special style of Rabbi Avraham de Boton [cite: 1]. His writing is characterized by clear, orderly, precise and rich Hebrew, which avoids rhetorical clumsiness and presents the legal argument in a logical, transparent and ordered manner [cite: 1]. This clear style contributed greatly to the acceptance of his rulings among the sages of later generations [cite: 1].
His Influence, Reception and Legacy for Generations
The Torah legacy of Rabbi Avraham de Boton has been deeply and fundamentally absorbed into the world of Jewish study [cite: 1, 2, 4]. Few are the works that have merited entering the status of permanent "carriers" (nosei keilim) printed alongside the foundational text [cite: 1, 2]. Beginning with the printing of the central editions of the book "Mishneh Torah" in Venice (such as the edition of 5462 / 1702), the "Lechem Mishneh" commentary was incorporated permanently alongside the "Kesef Mishneh" and the "Maggid Mishneh" [cite: 1, 4, 18]. This incorporation turned the "Lechem Mishneh" into a mandatory text for every student of the Rambam [cite: 1, 2]. Its ability to resolve severe difficulties and to reveal the hidden depth of the Rambam's rulings served as a model for later works, foremost the commentary "Mishneh LaMelech" by Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, which continued and expanded the theoretical path paved by the "Lechem Mishneh" [cite: 4, 8].
In the 19th and 20th centuries, with the rise of the yeshiva world in Lithuania and the development of the conceptual-analytical method of study, the "Lechem Mishneh" commentary experienced a renewed flourishing. The heads of yeshivot saw in the novellae of Rabbi Avraham de Boton the prototype of the conceptual distinction, since the "Lechem Mishneh" was among the first to show that contradictions in the Rambam do not stem merely from variant readings, but from different legal conceptions of the halakhic concept in different contexts [cite: 8, 13, 14]. In parallel, his responses in the book "Responsa Lechem Rav" became a first-rate source of authority in Sephardic and Ottoman halakhic rulings [cite: 3, 15]. The sages of Izmir, Salonika, Jerusalem and Constantinople cited his rulings on matters of communal ordinances, commercial customs, the laws of ketubot and marriage, and saw in him one of the fathers of the Ottoman legal tradition [cite: 3, 15].
Summary
Rabbi Chiya Avraham de Boton presents an exemplary figure of a Torah scholar and halakhic authority working at the historical meeting point between the Sephardic heritage and the Ottoman center in Salonika [cite: 1, 2]. Although he died with his days cut short, in a short time he succeeded in leaving an indelible mark on the Jewish bookshelf [cite: 1, 2]. His editorial decision not to duplicate what was written in the "Kesef Mishneh" of Rabbi Yosef Karo, but to create a concentrated, deep and complementary commentary, produced one of the most brilliant interpretive works on the Yad HaChazakah [cite: 1, 9, 10]. In his interpretive work in the "Lechem Mishneh" and in his halakhic responses in "Responsa Lechem Rav," Rabbi Avraham built a methodological bridge between plain meaning and the talmudic source on the one hand, and dialectic and conceptual depth on the other [cite: 3, 8, 13]. His legacy continues to resonate in the study halls and in halakhic literature to this very day, as an inseparable part of the study of the Rambam and the teaching of the sages of Salonika [cite: 1, 2, 4].
